```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, dpi = 100, fig.asp = 0.62, fig.width = 7,

library(mvgam)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(mvgam_theme(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif"))
```

Joint species distribution models (JSDMs) assign the species
co-occurrence that remains once the measured environment is accounted
for to a few latent factors (Warton et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2015.09.007); Ovaskainen et al.
[2017](https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.12757)). The loadings imply a
residual covariance among species. The factor scores ordinate the
sites.

`jsdgam()` fits this model with the loadings identified by a QR
rotation (Heaps and Jermyn
[2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-024-10454-0)). This article
fits it to counts of epigaeic ants at 30 sites in south-eastern
Australia (Gibb et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-014-3101-9)) and adds three
extensions in turn: environmental effects that act through the
factors, a loadings prior informed by species traits and a prior
under which the data decide how many factors are active.

## The data

`antTraits` from the mvabund package holds counts of 41 ant species
at 30 sites, five environmental covariates and five species traits.
Two traits are ordinal scores, which the code below converts to
numbers. `jsdgam()` takes one row per site and species:

```{r data}
data(antTraits, package = "mvabund")
abund <- antTraits$abund
env <- as.data.frame(scale(antTraits$env))
traits <- antTraits$traits
# Pilosity and polymorphism are scores stored as unordered factors
traits$Pilosity <- as.numeric(as.character(traits$Pilosity))
traits$Polymorphism <- as.numeric(as.character(traits$Polymorphism))

ant_data <- data.frame(
  site = rep(seq_len(nrow(abund)), times = ncol(abund)),
  species = factor(rep(colnames(abund), each = nrow(abund)),
                   levels = colnames(abund)),
  counts = as.vector(as.matrix(abund))
)
ant_data <- cbind(ant_data, env[ant_data$site, ])
```

Because the variance of each species' counts rises well above its
mean, the counts take a negative binomial family:

```{r mean-variance, fig.cap = "Mean and variance of each species' counts on log1p axes. The dashed line marks the equality a Poisson family would imply."}
moments <- data.frame(
  mean = tapply(ant_data$counts, ant_data$species, mean),
  var = tapply(ant_data$counts, ant_data$species, var)
)
ggplot(moments, aes(mean, var)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(colour = "#8F2727") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  labs(x = "Mean count", y = "Variance of counts")
```

## Latent factors alone

The first model leaves all structure among species to two latent
factors. `factor_formula = ~ -1` puts no covariates on the factors:

```{r mod-base}
mod_base <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)
```

`ordinate()` draws the posterior medians of the site scores and the
species loadings as a biplot:

```{r ordinate-base, fig.asp = 0.85, fig.cap = "Biplot of the site scores (numbered points) and species loadings (arrows) from the model with latent factors alone."}
ordinate(mod_base)
```

```{r base-numbers, include = FALSE}
# Squared length of each species' loading vector, which no rotation of
# the factors changes
z <- apply(as_draws_matrix(mod_base, variable = "Z_tilde", regex = TRUE),
           2, median)
sp <- sub("^Z_tilde\\[(.*),[0-9]+\\]$", "\\1", names(z))
norms <- sort(tapply(z^2, sp, sum), decreasing = TRUE)
lead <- gsub("\\.+", " ", names(norms)[1:2])
```

The loadings of `r lead[1]` and `r lead[2]` lie furthest from the
origin. Their abundances vary most across sites beyond what the
intercepts predict.

## Environmental effects on the factors

A constrained ordination lets the environment move the sites along
the factors. `lv_axis()` in `factor_formula` gives each factor its own
slope on a covariate. Each species then responds to the covariate
through its loadings, with two slopes per covariate in place of 41:

```{r mod-env}
mod_env <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1 + Bare.ground:lv_axis() +
    Canopy.cover:lv_axis() + Shrub.cover:lv_axis(),
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)
fixef(mod_env, trend_effects = TRUE)
```

`fixef()` reports the slopes in the same rotated basis as the
identified loadings `Z_tilde`. A species' response is the product of
its loadings and these slopes. `posterior_linpred()` returns it as the
change in each species' linear predictor between two sites that
differ only in canopy cover:

```{r canopy-responses}
newdata <- expand.grid(species = levels(ant_data$species),
                       Canopy.cover = c(0, 1))
newdata$site <- 1
newdata$Bare.ground <- 0
newdata$Shrub.cover <- 0
lp <- posterior_linpred(mod_env, newdata = newdata)
canopy <- lp[, newdata$Canopy.cover == 1] - lp[, newdata$Canopy.cover == 0]
canopy_q <- data.frame(
  species = levels(ant_data$species),
  t(apply(canopy, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)))
)
names(canopy_q)[2:4] <- c("lo", "med", "hi")
canopy_q$species <- reorder(canopy_q$species, canopy_q$med)
```

```{r canopy-plot, fig.asp = 1.1, fig.cap = "Posterior median and 95% credible interval of each species' response to one standard deviation of canopy cover, on the log scale of expected counts."}
ggplot(canopy_q, aes(med, species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), colour = "#8F2727",
                  size = 0.25) +
  labs(x = "Response to canopy cover", y = NULL)
```

```{r canopy-numbers, include = FALSE}
clear <- canopy_q$lo > 0 | canopy_q$hi < 0
top <- as.character(canopy_q$species[which.max(canopy_q$med)])
bottom <- as.character(canopy_q$species[which.min(canopy_q$med)])
# The prose below says both signs are present among the species whose
# interval excludes zero
stopifnot(any(canopy_q$lo > 0), any(canopy_q$hi < 0))
```

The intervals of `r sum(clear)` of the 41 species exclude zero. The
responses run from `r gsub("\\.+", " ", bottom)` (fewer ants under
canopy) to `r gsub("\\.+", " ", top)` (more).

## Trait-informed loadings

The default prior treats every species' loadings as independent. The
`traits` argument replaces it with the structured prior of Heaps and
Jermyn ([2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-024-10454-0)). Each
column of loadings is drawn from a multivariate normal whose
covariance among species comes from a kernel on the standardised
traits, with one length scale per trait. A short length scale lets
that trait separate species' loadings. A long one leaves them
exchangeable.

```{r mod-traits}
mod_traits <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 2,
  traits = traits,
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)
```

Each length scale is named for its trait:

```{r theta, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Posterior medians with 50% and 90% credible intervals of the length scale of each trait."}
mcmc_plot(mod_traits, variable = "theta_features", regex = TRUE,
          type = "intervals")
```

```{r theta-numbers, include = FALSE}
theta <- as_draws_matrix(mod_traits, variable = "theta_features",
                         regex = TRUE)
theta_med <- apply(theta, 2, median)
short <- which.min(theta_med)
shortest <- sub("theta_features_", "", names(theta_med)[short])
# The prose below says one trait's median length scale is smaller than
# every other trait's 5% quantile
stopifnot(theta_med[short] < min(apply(theta[, -short], 2, quantile, 0.05)))
```

The median length scale of `r gsub("\\.", " ", shortest)` falls below
the 5% quantile of every other trait's length scale. That trait carries most of the
information the prior takes from the traits. `compare_loadings()`
aligns the two fits' loadings by a Procrustes rotation and draws how
far each species moved:

```{r compare-loadings, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Posterior median loadings of each species without and with the trait prior, aligned to a shared basis. Labels mark the ten species that moved furthest."}
compare_loadings(mod_base, mod_traits,
                 labels = c("uninformed", "trait-informed"),
                 label_species = "shift")
```

Leave-one-out cross-validation compares the two priors on the same
likelihood:

```{r loo}
loo_cmp <- loo_compare(list(uninformed = loo(mod_base),
                            `trait-informed` = loo(mod_traits)))
loo_cmp
```

```{r loo-numbers, include = FALSE}
# The prose below says the trait prior predicts better by more than
# twice the standard error of the difference
stopifnot(rownames(loo_cmp)[1] == "trait-informed",
          -loo_cmp[2, "elpd_diff"] > 2 * loo_cmp[2, "se_diff"])
fe_diff <- sprintf("%.1f", -loo_cmp[2, "elpd_diff"])
fe_se <- sprintf("%.1f", loo_cmp[2, "se_diff"])
```

With the trait prior the model predicts held-out counts better, by
`r fe_diff` (SE `r fe_se`) in expected log predictive density.

## Residual correlations

`residual_cor()` summarises the posterior residual correlation
between every pair of species. `plot(cluster = TRUE)` orders the
species to bring blocks of co-occurring species onto the diagonal:

```{r resid-cor, fig.asp = 1, out.width = "95%", fig.cap = "Posterior median residual correlations from the trait-informed model. Outlined cells have 95% intervals excluding zero."}
rcor <- residual_cor(mod_traits)
plot(rcor, cluster = TRUE)
```

```{r cor-numbers, include = FALSE}
pairs <- upper.tri(rcor$cor)
clear_pos <- sum(rcor$cor_lower[pairs] > 0)
clear_neg <- sum(rcor$cor_upper[pairs] < 0)
stopifnot(clear_pos > 0, clear_neg > 0)
```

Of the `r sum(pairs)` species pairs, `r clear_pos` correlate
positively and `r clear_neg` negatively with intervals that exclude
zero. A residual correlation may reflect a shared
response to an unmeasured driver or an interaction between species.
The model alone cannot tell the two apart.

## How many factors?

The models so far fixed two factors. A multiplicative gamma process
prior (Bhattacharya and Dunson
[2011](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asr013)) shrinks each column of
loadings more strongly than the one before. With a generous ceiling,
the data decide how many columns stay away from zero. The prior
combines with the trait kernel through `loadings_prior`:

```{r mod-mgp}
mod_mgp <- jsdgam(
  counts ~ 1,
  factor_formula = ~ -1,
  data = ant_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  n_lv = 6,
  loadings_prior = list(column_shrinkage = "mgp", features = traits),
  unit = site,
  species = species,
  chains = 4, seed = 2025, silent = 2
)
```

`active_factors()` applies the cumulative shrinkage criterion of
Legramanti et al. ([2020](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asaa008)): a
column is active when its squared norm exceeds 1% of the leading
column's with posterior probability above one half.

```{r active-factors, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "Posterior probability that each column of loadings is active. The dashed line marks the threshold."}
af <- active_factors(mod_mgp)
plot(af)
```

```{r af-numbers, include = FALSE}
n_active <- sum(af$per_factor$is_active)
stopifnot(n_active > 2, n_active < 6)
```

`r n_active` of the six columns are active. The earlier two-factor
models held the residual structure in a smaller latent space than the
data support.

## Summary

Traits and column shrinkage both changed what the ant community model
concluded. The trait prior predicted held-out counts better than
independent loadings, by `r fe_diff` in expected log predictive
density against a standard error of `r fe_se`. The shrinkage prior
found `r n_active` active factors where the first models assumed two.
Each extension is one argument to a single `jsdgam()` call, as are
the environmental slopes that gave all 41 species a canopy response
from three covariates.

## Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as `?jsdgam`,
`?lv_axis` or `?ordinate`, with its arguments and output.
`how_to_cite()` writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model, naming
the architecture it used. `jsdgam()` also takes a phylogeny through
`phylo`, trait-mediated environmental responses through
`trait_slopes` and imperfect detection through the `occ()` family.

Related articles:

- [Dynamic factor models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/dfm.html)
  give the factors dynamics over time.
- [N-mixture models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/nmix.html)
  cover the closure-unit families that `occ()` belongs to.
- [mvgam overview](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/mvgam_overview.html)
  introduces the observation and trend formulas.
